headlines.summary: Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo is drawing early demand as analysts assess whether the foldable can lift iPhone pricing and revenue.
headlines.article_text: Apple iPhone Duo demand, pricing and revenue impact Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Apple's iPhone Duo launch-day pickup inventory sold out quickly, with some delivery estimates already slipping into late January online. The price of the first foldable iPhone reaches $3,199 at 2TB, creating a new tier above the Pro and Pro Max. Analysts say the Duo could boost Apple’s average selling prices through trade-ups, Android switchers and a halo effect across the rest of the iPhone lineup. In this article AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:19 02:19 First impressions of the iPhone Duo — Apple's biggest iPhone redesign ever News Videos Apple 's iPhone Duo , its most expensive iPhone ever, went up for preorder Friday, with launch-day pickup inventory selling out and some online delivery estimates already slipping into late January. The company said in a statement that the preorder demand was "nothing short of extraordinary." "We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online," Apple said. Apple's first foldable phone starts at $1,999 and passes $3,000 at the 2TB storage tier. It is the biggest change to the physical design of the iPhone in years and establishes an entirely new price point above the Pro and Pro Max. The early rush offers a first glimpse at the demand behind Apple's bet: Whether a dramatic new design can persuade customers to spend more and push the iPhone even further as a status symbol. But analysts who spoke with CNBC said Apple's bet is not that foldables suddenly become a mass-market product. It is that a relatively small group of its highest-spending customers can become significantly more valuable. Foldables are expected to make up just over 2% of global smartphone units this year but nearly 7% of industry revenue, according to IDC. By 2030, IDC expects the category to account for 10% of smartphone revenue while still representing only about 3% of units. That gap between volume and value is central to Apple's opportunity. "Duo is fast becoming an aspirational foldable," IDC's Nabila Popal told CNBC, comparing its appeal with Apple's broader position as an aspirational smartphone brand. Apple CEO John Ternus, alongside vice president of industrial design Molly Anderson, shows off the new iPhone Duo during an Apple event at the Steve Jobs Theater in Apple Park in Cupertino, California, Sept. 9, 2026. Karl Mondon | Afp | Getty Images Popal, global senior research director for the Consumer Device Team at IDC, said the technology itself is not necessarily the breakthrough. Foldable Android phones have existed for years. What's new is Apple bringing that form factor to the enormous base of consumers already invested in the iPhone ecosystem. Apple itself has been exploring the form factor for more than a decade. In 2011, Ternus and five other Apple engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, according to a recent Time profile. "It's not that it's a breakthrough or new technology, but it's from Apple," Popal said. The Duo could also prove more accessible than some industry watchers had anticipated. Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights who attended Apple's launch event, said many expected the foldable iPhone to start between $2,400 and $2,500. Apple coming in at $1,999, Sag said, suggests the company "wants a lot of share." Sag expects the Duo to become "very much a status symbol" during the holiday season and potentially into next year. That status appeal could be reinforced by scarcity. Apple has an installed base of roughly 1.4 billion iPhones, he noted, meaning even a small percentage of early adopters could overwhelm the roughly 6 million or fewer units Counterpoint expects to be available in the near term. IDC also expects supply to be constrained initially because of the complexity of the device and Apple's manufacturing and quality standards. "Exclusivity is part of the current appeal," Popal said. And Apple has made explicit luxury plays before. When the first Apple Watch launched, the company offered the 18-karat gold Edition starting at $10,000. Apple also formed a long-running partnership with Hermès around premium watch bands and designs. That push came during the tenure of Angela Ahrendts, the former Burberry CEO who joined Apple in 2014 to lead retail and online stores, as the company experimented with bringing more of the language and presentation of luxury fashion into its stores and products. The Duo takes that idea into Apple's largest product business. Low volume, high value IDC expects Apple to ship roughly 7 million units this year, or roughly 3% of Apple's total shipments in 2026. Popal, the IDC analyst, forecasts Duo shipments could grow another 70% next year. That would give Apple roughly 40% of the global foldable market and would make it the category's largest player, surpassing Samsung and Huawei. According to her forecast, Apple could ship as many Duos in the next six months as the previous category leaders did in all of 2025. But the more important number for Apple may not be units. A large share of Duo customers are expected to be existing iPhone owners, analysts said, including consumers who otherwise might have purchased a Pro Max and are now trading up to a device costing hundreds of dollars more. Others could add the Duo as a second smartphone, with Apple's ecosystem allowing users to move relatively seamlessly between it and their primary iPhone. Popal said that migration from roughly $1,200 premium iPhones to a device starting at nearly $2,000 should provide a "healthy boost" to Apple's revenue even if overall volumes remain relatively small. watch now VIDEO 2:02 02:02 Apple's iPhone Duo goes on sale: Here's what you need to know TechCheck JPMorgan reached a similar conclusion. The bank expects the Duo to have a disproportionate impact on iPhone revenue because of its much higher average selling price, even as overall iPhone shipments are expected to remain roughly flat next year. JPMorgan said the iPhone 18 cycle is increasingly likely to be driven by price and product mix rather than unit growth. D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said Apple needs the Duo to succeed as it comes up against a difficult set of earnings comps with its strongest upgrade cycle in years. "Without an uplift from Duo, they may experience some pretty pedestrian revenue growth," Luria told CNBC. The device gives Apple several ways to generate that uplift, he added. It raises the company's average selling price by capturing die-hard Apple customers who might otherwise have bought a Pro Max. It could bring in some consumers who previously bought folding Android phones because Apple did not offer one. And it could create a halo around the rest of the iPhone lineup. Luria said some consumers will visit Apple stores specifically to see the Duo, "but probably walk out with an iPhone or iPhone Pro at half the price." That means the Duo can potentially help Apple even when someone decides not to buy it. Lead times for the iPhone 18 Pro have softened in several markets compared with the prior cycle, while the more expensive Pro Max has held up better, according to JPMorgan's tracking. Musk said any restrictions on Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine would have come from decisions by the president or White House. Andrew Harnik | Getty Images President Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces. Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield , a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government." Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour. Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions." Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX. "Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote . "As your European customers, we are watching you." Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian. The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions. Reuters reported on Thursday , citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order. On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far." Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday. SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday.
